title: When to reorder and what to control

scenes.title: When to reorder and what to control
scenes.subtitle: Reorder point, safety stock and ABC analysis
narration: Welcome to lesson two.
The EOQ told us how much to order. Now we answer two more questions: when should we order, and which items deserve the most attention?

scenes.definition: The inventory level at which a new order is placed.
scenes.gloss: A line on the shelf: when stock falls to it, you place the next order.

points.text: **L**: lead time, in days, from order to delivery
**SS**: safety stock, extra stock against uncertainty in demand or lead time

narration: Your notes define the reorder point as the inventory level at which a new order is placed.
Think of it as a line drawn on the shelf. When stock falls to that line, you place the next order.
It depends on daily demand, d, and the lead time, L, which is the number of days the supplier takes to deliver.
And on safety stock, the extra stock a firm keeps because demand or delivery time can surprise it.

scenes.heading: The reorder point formula
narration: Here is the formula from page six. The reorder point equals d times L, plus S S.
d times L is the stock you will use up while you wait for the delivery to arrive.
Safety stock is the cushion on top, in case demand rises or the truck is late.
So you order early enough that the new stock lands just as you reach your cushion.

scenes.heading: Example 2: the reorder point
narration: Let's apply it to the same distributor, in Example 2 on page six. Demand is {{D}} units a year over {{WD}} working days, the lead time is {{L}} days, and the safety stock is {{SS}} units.
First, daily demand: {{D}} divided by {{WD}} is {{d}} units a day.
During the {{L}} day lead time, the firm uses {{d}} times {{L}}, which is {{DL}} units.
Add the safety stock of {{SS}} units.

narration.text: The reorder point is {{ROP}} units. When stock falls to {{ROP}}, the distributor places a new order of {{EOQ|0}} units.

scenes.heading: Reorder point on the stock chart

notes.text: Stock never planned to fall below **safety stock**.
At **260 units**, order. The delivery takes **5 days**.
It arrives as stock reaches the cushion.

narration: Here is the same idea on a chart. Each order of {{EOQ|0}} units lifts the stock, and demand uses it up.
The orange line is the reorder point, {{ROP}} units. The moment stock touches it, an order goes out.
The red line is the safety stock of {{SS}} units. Under normal demand, stock should not fall below it.
Five days later, the new order arrives, just as stock reaches the cushion. This chart is drawn from the numbers in Example 2.

scenes.heading: ABC analysis: not every item deserves equal attention
narration: Page seven introduces ABC analysis. Items are classified by annual consumption value, which is annual demand times unit cost, following the Pareto principle.
Class A items are only ten to twenty percent of the items, but seventy to eighty percent of the value. They get tight control and frequent review.
Class B is about thirty percent of items and fifteen to twenty five percent of the value, with moderate control.
Class C is fifty to sixty percent of the items, yet only five to ten percent of the value, so simple control and bulk ordering are enough.

scenes.heading: The limitation: value is not the same as importance

items.text: A cheap item can still be **critical**: it may stop production
So firms combine ABC with **VED**: Vital, Essential, Desirable

callout.title: A hospital pharmacy
callout.text: Cotton and saline are low-value class C items. But run out, and surgeries stop. VED marks them Vital, so they are always kept in stock.

narration: Your notes also give the limitation. ABC looks only at value.
A cheap item can still be critical, because running out of it may stop production.
So firms combine ABC with VED analysis, which grades items as vital, essential or desirable.
Here is an example of my own, not from your notes. In a hospital pharmacy, cotton and saline are cheap class C items, but without them surgeries stop, so they are treated as vital.

scenes.heading: Three inventory decisions

steps.label: Where to focus?
steps.title: ABC analysis
steps.text: Tight control for the few high-value A items

narration: Your notes end with a summary, and it fits together as three decisions. How much to order: the E O Q balances ordering and holding cost.
When to order: the reorder point, d times L plus safety stock.
And where to focus control: ABC analysis, combined with VED for critical items.

scenes.heading: Remember

items.text: A items: few items, most of the value; tight control
Combine ABC with VED for cheap but critical items

narration: To recap: the reorder point is d times L plus safety stock.
In Example 2, that is forty times five plus sixty, which is {{ROP}} units.
In ABC analysis, A items are few but carry most of the value, so they get the tightest control.
And combine ABC with VED, so that cheap but critical items are never missing. That completes Unit 3.
